Pass the Hash 001 — a guided SOC investigation
  1 / 1
Start●

You have been handed an alert. Work out what happened.

no experience needed

This is the alert your security team woke up to. Read it before you touch anything:

The alertMultiple distinct accounts authenticating to one server from a single source - one workstation (10.0.4.10) signed in to the target server sec-win-03 as several different privileged accounts in quick succession, all logon type 3, including an explicit-credential logon (Windows event 4648) against a service account, and minutes later that workstation made a high-volume SMB read (port 445) from an internal file server.

Your job is to decide one thing: is this a real attack that must be escalated, or a false alarm that can be closed? You will answer it the way a real analyst does — not by guessing, but by following the evidence from the first search to the last and writing down what you find as you go. By the final card you will know who broke in, how, to which machines, what they took, and when.

What this guide is

It starts at zeroNo security knowledge and no Elastic experience needed. The investigation itself is clicking and reading; the only typing is your report, at the end.
The pictures are realEvery screen picture in this guide is a photograph of the running lab, taken by screenshotting the real Kibana. Nothing is drawn from memory.
It never leaves you guessingAfter every click it says the exact number or text you should now be looking at, and a numbered circle points at the control.
It cleans up after itselfOne file starts the lab — setup-lab.cmd on Windows, setup-lab.sh on macOS or Linux — and one removes it completely. Nothing is left behind.

The one thing you need first

Docker, installed and running — Docker Desktop on Windows or macOS, Docker Engine on Linux. That is the only prerequisite. The lab runs inside it and installs nothing else on your computer. If you do not have Docker yet, ask your instructor — this lab assumes it is already there.

Prep1

The words you need to know

read once

You will see all of these in the tool and in your report. Read them once now and the rest of the lab becomes much easier.

The attack

NTLM hashWindows never stores your password in a form anyone can read backwards. It stores an NTLM hash: a fixed-length fingerprint. Tools such as Mimikatz copy that hash out of a running machine's memory. Anyone holding the hash does not need to crack it.
Pass-the-hash (PtH)Handing the stolen hash to the authentication service as if it were the password. Windows accepts it. The attacker never learns the real password and never has to break anything — which is exactly why this technique is so fast and so common.
Event 4648“A user was explicitly assigned the primary credential.” A normal logon reuses a credential Windows already had; a 4648 means the caller deliberately handed the credential over. In healthy traffic this record is nearly absent, so finding one is itself the finding.
Logon type 3Recorded in logon.type. A network logon: the user is somewhere else and authenticated over the LAN. A replayed hash always looks like this. Type 2 would be someone at the machine's own keyboard.
Service accountA non-human login used by software, named like svc_backup or ending in $. Service accounts belong to scheduled jobs, never to a person typing at a keyboard, so seeing one in an interactive-looking login sequence is a red flag on its own.
SMB, port 445The Windows file-sharing protocol. It always uses 445, and the network.bytes field tells you how much data moved in the session.

The tool

AlertA rule that fires when something looks dangerous. It is a hint, not a fact. Investigators confirm or dismiss it.
ElasticsearchThe database that stores and searches the logs. Answers web addresses like localhost:9200.
KibanaThe website you do all the work in, sitting on top of Elasticsearch. Lives at localhost:5601.
Data viewKibana’s word for “which pile shall I look at”. Older versions called it an index pattern. Ours are auth-* and network-*.
DiscoverThe Kibana screen where you type a search and read the matching log lines. You will spend all your time here.
DocumentOne single log record. There are 274 in the auth pile and 146 in network. This is what you read.
FieldOne labelled box inside a document, like user.name. The part before the dot is the group.
KQLThe query language you type into Kibana’s search bar. field: value means “field equals value”, and and joins two conditions.
True positiveThe attack is real. Escalate it, contain it, tell someone.
False positiveNothing bad happened. Close the alert with a note saying why not.

The three fields that matter most

Almost every question in this investigation is answered by three fields. Learn these and the whole lab is just typing:

  • event.code — the number of the Windows log record. It tells you what kind of thing happened. You only need three of them:
    4624 = an account was successfully logged on  ·  4625 = a logon failed  ·  4648 = a credential was explicitly assigned
  • source.ip — the address the record came from. This is the machine that made the connection. Your pivot field.
  • host.name — the server the event was recorded on. A logon is “from a source.ip and on a host.name”, and getting those two the wrong way round is the difference between the right answer and no answer at all.
The shape of the attack, before you see it

A pass-the-hash attack always has the same four beats: one machine authenticates as many different accounts in a very short time, one of those logins is recorded as an explicit-credential logon, one of the accounts is not a person but a service account, and it then reads something. Hold that pattern in your head. By the middle of this lab you will be hunting for exactly those four things.

The one thing that stops most people

Docker must be installed and running. The lab runs both programs inside Docker containers. If the setup file says docker was not found, or that it is installed but not running, start it — Docker Desktop on Windows or macOS, Docker Engine on Linux — wait until it says it is running, then run the file again. That one check fixes almost every startup problem.

What you should see

A black window that works through ten numbered stages. It verifies its own work as it goes, so the last thing it prints before the addresses looks like this:

The end of the setup file's own verification query 1 every successful logon that day = 53 query 2 the explicit-credential logon = 1 query 3 every logon on the target server = 5 query 4 the rule's own query = 5 query 5 the smb file read = 1 distinct accounts replayed onto sec-win-03 = 5 the smb session that moved over 900 KB = 1 smb sessions aimed at the file server 10.0.4.12 = 1 the trap count, with the event code dropped = 6 [verify] every number the walkthrough quotes matches the live index.

Those numbers are the answers to this whole investigation. The script has already proved them against the live index, which is why you can trust every count in the rest of this guide. Then it prints:

The last thing the setup file prints The lab is ready. Elasticsearch : http://127.0.0.1:9200 Kibana : http://127.0.0.1:5601 data view "auth" index pattern auth-* data view "network" index pattern network-*

What it did for you while you waited

So the output does not frighten you, the script performed exactly the jobs that would otherwise be the hard part of this lab:

  • Started two programs — Elasticsearch (the database) and Kibana (the website).
  • Taught Elasticsearch what each field means. An index template declares “event.code holds a number” and “source.ip holds a network address” before any data arrives. Without it Elasticsearch guesses, and guessing quietly breaks your searches.
  • Loaded the log data. If it had already loaded it, it says so and imports nothing — your data cannot load twice.
  • Created your two data views and then read them back to prove the index pattern really was stored. A data view with an empty pattern matches nothing at all, and the cause of that is invisible, so the script checks it instead of hoping.
  • Installed the detection rule and waited for it to fire. The alert you are about to read did not exist until the script did that, and the script does not print ready until the alerts are really there — 5 of them. If the rule had matched nothing, you would have been told so instead of being handed an empty page.

What you are looking at

Do this

  2. Look at Alerts by name: one rule, count 5. That is five separate events, not one summary.

What one alert says

Two different times, and the difference matters

The alert’s own timestamp is when the rule ran — a minute or two ago, because the rule is still running every minute. The log record underneath it happened on 22 September 2026. So the alerts are new and the events they point at are old, and the alerts page will keep showing them while Discover, which looks at the events themselves, shows you nothing at all until you set its time range. That is the next card, and it is not a fault.

You are not imagining it, and nothing has gone wrong. Open any alert on the JSON tab and you will find two clocks on it:

The two timestamps, from one alert@timestamp the day YOU ran this kibana.alert.original_time 2026-09-22T14:05:00.000Z the moment of the attack

@timestamp is when Elastic noticed. It is the day you ran the setup file, so it is a different date for every batch and it tells you nothing about the attack. kibana.alert.original_time is when the activity actually happened, and that one never moves — for this lab it is always 22 September. So: an alert is a claim that something happened; the original time is the evidence for it. Every real SOC works this way, because logs often arrive late or a rule is run against history, and if alerts were dated by the event, today’s real alerts would be buried under a wall of old ones.

Which one goes in your report? The original time. Every time you write in this lab, write the time of the activity, never the time the tool noticed it.

If the table is empty, it is the time picker

Not a broken lab. An alert is stamped with the time it was raised, so the range this page starts on — Today, meaning from midnight — stops covering it once you cross midnight. Click the time picker at the top right and set it to 1 unit Days. The five alerts come back. Some versions put a ready-made Last 24 hours button there instead, which does the same job. The lab itself never changed.

What you should have now

One rule, five critical alerts, risk score 99, all raised against records from 10.0.4.10 on sec-win-03. You have not run a single query yet and you already know the shape of the attack: one machine, several identities, one server.

Alert is running4

Read the rule that fired

2 minutes, well spent

Worth seeing, because the rule and your own investigation are the same filter. When the two agree, you know you have not just found the answer — you have found what the monitoring system found, by a different road.

Do this

  1. Open the hamburger menu (☰) in the top left, then Security → Rules. That is the page of detection rules.
  2. Find the rule called Multiple distinct accounts authenticating to one server from a single source. It is the only custom rule you have, so the Custom rules (1) filter is already showing it.
  3. Read its Last run status. It says Success, and Last run is seconds ago — the rule runs once a minute.

Read its query

Click the rule name to open it, then find the Query box. It reads, character for character:

The rule's own query — this is Query 4 of this guideevent.code: 4624 and host.name: "sec-win-03" and source.ip: "10.0.4.10"
Why this is worth two minutes

Because it means the alert count and your query count have to agree. The rule says 5, so when Query 4 later returns 5 you have not merely found the same answer twice — you have found the same answer the monitoring system found, by a different road. If the two numbers ever disagree, one of them is wrong, and now you know which one to trust.

A rule is a claim, not a conclusion

Notice what the rule does not say. It does not say “attack”. It says five successful logons, to this server, from this address. Whether that is a routine maintenance window or a compromise is the part you are here to answer, and the rule has deliberately told you nothing about it.

Your browser just opened. Here is why the screen is empty.

not broken

You have read the alert. Now come to Discover, where the investigation happens — click the hamburger menu (☰) in the top left and then Discover. This card exists because this screen looks broken, and it is not — the attack was three weeks ago and Discover is looking at the last few minutes, so it is simply showing you nothing yet. Here is the real screen, exactly as you are looking at it now:

Do not click “Try ES|QL” — here is what happens if you do

This build of Kibana includes ES|QL, a different query language, and the Try ES|QL button is an advert for it aimed at people who already know their way around. If you click it you will land on a screen showing this:

The error you will seeFROM logs-*-*,logs-*,filebeat-* | WHERE @timestamp >= ?_tstart AND @timestamp <= ?_tend | LIMIT 10 Unknown index [logs-*-*,logs-*,filebeat-*]

That query looks for indices called logs-* and filebeat-*. Our lab has no such indices — it has auth-* and network-*. So the query cannot work and that error is expected. It does not mean the lab is broken, and there is nothing for you to fix.

What to do instead: press the browser’s Back button to return to the screen above, then carry on. This guide only ever uses the KQL search bar.

So what is wrong right now?

Exactly one thing: the time range. The data view may need changing, but that is the card after this one. The logs are simply older than the last fifteen minutes.

That is the single most common reason a beginner meets an empty screen. The Search entire time range button fixes it for you. Two cards from now you will also learn to do the same thing by hand, so you can pin an exact window rather than “everything”.

Pick a pile6

Choose which pile of logs to look at

which logs?2 min

First, tell Discover which pile of logs to read. You have two, and only one of them is where this attack starts.

Do this

  1. Click the dropdown on the far left of the search bar — the control with the label Data view beside it. It may read Default security data view.
  2. Look at the list that opens. There are only two entries that are yours, and this is what it looks like:
The two entries that matter, and what is in them
Data viewDocumentsHolds
auth-*274Logons (4624), explicit-credential logons (4648), failed logons (4625), logoffs (4634), privilege assignment (4672), lockouts (4740), Kerberos pre-auth failures (4771), process starts (4688)
network-*146Connections between machines: SMB, RPC, DNS, LDAP, HTTP, SSH, ICMP

The * is a wildcard meaning “anything starting with auth”, so a single entry covers every day of auth logs. If you ever see a third entry you do not recognise, leave it alone and pick auth-*.

You will still see no documents after closing this panel. That is correct — the time range is still the last 15 minutes. The next card fixes that.

Why this matters

A data view is a bookmark. It tells Kibana which pile of documents to read and which field holds the time. Pick the wrong one and a perfectly good query returns nothing at all, because the documents it is looking for are not in that pile.

So whenever a query returns zero results, check these three things in this order: the data view, then the time range, then the query itself. Nine times out of ten it is one of the first two, never the third.

If the sidebar says “no available fields” and stays that way

Then the data views were not created properly. Do not fight it — run the setup file again. It is safe to run twice, it reloads nothing, and it verifies each data view and tells you if anything is wrong instead of printing a hopeful message.

If you would rather pin the exact day by hand

Both methods give the same 274 documents, because every record in this lab happened inside 22 September 2026. But if you want a fixed window you can type yourself, click the left half of the time range (the start date) and the absolute editor opens:

The one thing that will look “wrong”: Kibana prints times in your timezone

Every timestamp in this lab is stored in UTC, and every picture in this guide was taken on a computer set to UTC. But the @timestamp column, the histogram axis and the friendly dates inside a document all follow your own computer’s timezone, and no setting inside Kibana changes that. If your machine is 8 hours ahead of UTC, the first logon that this guide calls Sep 22, 2026 @ 14:05:00.000 will appear in your table as Sep 23, 2026 @ 06:05:00.000.

So which is right? Both, and it does not matter. Here is the rule that keeps you out of trouble:

  • Read the clock times off your own screen and write down what you see. Your timeline will be internally consistent, which is all a timeline needs.
  • Trust the gaps, not the absolute numbers. Every conclusion in this guide is about how far apart things are, and a timezone shift moves every time by the same amount. The gaps — 4 minutes, 4, 4, 2, then 6 — are identical in every timezone on earth.
  • The gaps are the evidence. The burst is 14 minutes long. The file read is 6 minutes after the last logon. Write those down and you are right in any timezone.

Here is the one table you need if you want to convert a time this guide quotes. Find your own offset, then add or subtract it:

Your computer isExample citiesThen 14:05:00 UTC shows as
UTC+0Lagos, London in winterSep 22 @ 14:05:00
UTC+1Berlin, Paris, MadridSep 22 @ 15:05:00
UTC+2Cairo, Helsinki, JohannesburgSep 22 @ 16:05:00
UTC+5:30India, ColomboSep 22 @ 19:35:00
UTC+8Singapore, Beijing, Perth, Kuala LumpurSep 22 @ 22:05:00
UTC+9Tokyo, SeoulSep 22 @ 23:05:00
UTC−5New York, TorontoSep 22 @ 09:05:00
UTC−6Chicago, Mexico CitySep 22 @ 08:05:00
UTC−8Los Angeles, VancouverSep 22 @ 06:05:00

Not sure what your offset is? Compare the first bar of your histogram with the 00:00 printed under the left edge. Whatever the difference is, that is your offset. Or simply set your computer’s timezone to UTC before you start — then every picture in this guide matches your screen exactly. Not required. But it removes a whole category of confusion.

What you should have now — the whole lab opens up
  • The Documents tab reads Documents (274).
  • The blue histogram appears with a low line of bars across the day and one tall bar at 14:00. That is your instant visual proof you are looking at the right day.
  • The sidebar lists 17 available fields with a coloured letter beside each one — k for keyword, # for number, t for text, a calendar for dates, and a red box for IP addresses. Those letters tell you what each field can be asked to do.
Remember this one, and it will save you hours

An empty screen in Kibana is almost never a broken query. It is almost always the time range or the data view. Check those two first, every time.

And beware: if you ever press F5 to reload, or wander off to another page and come back, the time range can snap back to Last 15 minutes and the screen goes empty again. That is not your fault and it is not broken — just click Search entire time range again. Some analysts keep the working Discover tab open in a bookmark for exactly this reason.

Investigate8

Query 1 — the baseline: every logon that day

1 of 5 queries3 min
Why you are running this query

Before you can say something is unusual, you have to know what normal looks like. 4624 is the record written every time any account anywhere signs in, and in a real Windows estate it is one of the most common records that exist.

So this query deliberately produces a number that tells you nothing. Running it teaches you something worth more than the number: the event code on its own is not a finding.

Do this

Click inside the search bar, select whatever is in it, and paste in exactly this — then press Enter:

Search 1 — type this, then press Enterevent.code: 4624
What 53 actually tells you

53 successful logons happened across the whole estate that day, and they are smeared evenly from 00:00 to 23:00. There is no cluster, nothing at any particular moment, and the accounts repeat — jdoe and rneuman both appear more than once, and the servers are scattered across sec-win-01, sec-win-04 and sec-win-06.

That is exactly what healthy sign-in traffic looks like: people arriving at work, locking and unlocking their machines, signing on to servers. If you stop here and write “logons look normal”, you will be right, and you will also have found nothing.

What to do next, and why

You cannot see a shape inside a smear. To find the burst you have to stop counting everybody and start counting one server at a time — and the alert has already told you which one: sec-win-03.

Baseline9

Count the baseline, field by field

the other tab3 min

Kibana has a tool for exactly this question: how is this result set spread out? It is also how you will prove, two cards from now, that the five logons really are five different accounts.

Do this

  1. Leave the search bar exactly as it is: event.code: 4624.
  2. Click the Field statistics tab. It is a tab, immediately to the right of Documents (53) — not a section further down the page.
  3. Read the Distinct values column for host.name, logon.type and user.name.
The baseline, in four numbers
FieldDistinct valuesWhat it means
event.code1All 53 really are 4624. Your filter did what you asked.
host.name4The 53 logons were spread over four servers. Nothing concentrates.
logon.type4Types 2, 3, 7 and 11 all appear — keyboard, network, unlock and cached. A genuinely mixed day.
user.name7Seven different accounts across 53 logons, so each one signed in several times. That is repetition, and repetition is normal.

Four servers, four logon types, seven accounts, smeared over twenty-four hours. That is a normal Tuesday. There is nothing here to escalate, and no amount of staring at these 53 records will produce something that is not there.

But remember the method, because it is the same one that closes the case later: if the row count equals the distinct-value count, then every row is a different value. Right now 53 rows and 7 users — nothing unusual. Watch what happens when you run that same test on Query 3.

Why a baseline is the most useful thing in this lab

Almost every bad alert analysis in the real world dies right here. Somebody queries the scary event code, gets a large number, and then either panics and escalates noise, or shrugs and closes a real incident. Both are mistakes, and both come from stopping at this screen.

You now know what “normal sign-in activity” looks like, because you have seen it counted. That is a baseline, and you cannot spot an anomaly without one. Everything from here narrows down to one server, and every step from here has a small number you can check.

The rare one10

Query 2 — the rarest event in the whole estate

2 of 5 queries4 min
Why you are running this query

You have proved that a busy day looks like a busy day. Now go to the other end of the scale: the record that in healthy traffic is almost absent.

Your hypothesis is an explicit-credential logon — somebody handing a hash to Windows as if it were a password. This query either shows you that or it does not. There is no third outcome.

Do this

Replace the contents of the search bar with this, and press Enter:

Search 2 — type this, then press Enterevent.code: 4648

Add four columns so the row is readable: in the left sidebar, hover a field name until a + appears, and click it for user.name, host.name, source.ip and logon.type. Click the same + again to remove a column if you change your mind.

What this one row proves
  • Exactly one explicit-credential logon in the entire day. The tab says Documents (1). In a healthy estate this record would be zero.
  • The account is svc_backup — a service account. Not a person. Service accounts belong to scheduled jobs, and one appearing in an interactive-looking login sequence is a signal in its own right.
  • The target is sec-win-03 and the source is 10.0.4.10 — exactly the two values the alert named.
  • It is logon.type 3, at 14:19:00.000.

Write the account name down. It goes in your findings, and you will meet it two more times.

Get the detail11

Open the record and read the sentence at the bottom

the right button3 min

The table shows you a summary. For the exact values — and for the one field the summary does not show at all — you need to open the record.

Never click the row. Click the little arrow.

Each row has a small button with two arrows pointing diagonally away from each other (⇉), in a narrow column immediately to the left of the @timestamp column. Click that. Clicking anywhere else in the row does nothing at all — this is the single most common stumble in this lab, and it makes people think the lab is broken.

Do this

  1. On the single row, click the ⇉ two-diagonal-arrows button at its far left.
  2. A panel titled Document slides in from the right. Scroll it down to the message row at the bottom — it is a full English sentence, and it is the field the table summary hides.
The message field, in full
The whole sentence, exactly as the log records itA user was explicitly assigned the primary credential. Subject: CORP\ws-fin-01$. Target Account: svc_backup. Target Domain: CORP. Logon Type: 3 (network). Source Network Address: 10.0.4.10. Authentication Package: NTLM.

Four facts in one sentence, and every one of them is new:

FieldValue on this recordWhat it tells you
event.code4,648It is an explicit-credential logon. (Kibana prints it with a thousands separator; the real value is 4648.)
event.actionexplicit_credential_logonThe same fact, in words.
user.namesvc_backupA service account, not a person.
user.domainCORPYour domain.
host.namesec-win-03The target server — the one the credential was used against.
source.ip10.0.4.10Where it came from. Also named ws-fin-01 elsewhere in these logs.
logon.type3A network logon. Nobody was at the target’s keyboard.
source.port49,712Remember it. The last row of Query 3 uses the same port.
messageA user was explicitly assigned the primary credential. Subject: CORP\ws-fin-01$. Target Account: svc_backup. Target Domain: CORP. Logon Type: 3 (network). Source Network Address: 10.0.4.10. Authentication Package: NTLM.The whole record in one sentence.

Four things to take from it. First, the credential was supplied on purpose by a caller — the Subject is CORP\ws-fin-01$, and that trailing $ is how Windows writes a computer account. A machine handed its own credentials to the logon service. Second, the authentication package was NTLM, the older protocol that hashes can be replayed against. Third, nothing failed: there is no failed logon, no lockout, no brute force. Fourth, the target was a service account — so this is not one person signing in from a stolen laptop, it is software’s identity being used by something that is not software.

Getting back to the table

Click Close at the bottom of the panel, or the × at its top right, or just press Escape. Your columns and your sort order stay exactly as they were.

Narrow it12

Query 3 — every logon to the target server

3 of 5 queries5 min
Why you are running this query

You have found one deliberate hash replay. Now find out how far it went.

This query lists every successful logon recorded on sec-win-03 for the whole day. Every one of them is a moment the machine 10.0.4.10 became somebody on that server.

Do this — two parts

  1. Replace the contents of the search bar with this, and press Enter:
Search 3 — type this, then press Enterevent.code: 4624 and host.name: "sec-win-03"

Clause by clause: event.code: 4624 keeps only successful logons; host.name: "sec-win-03" keeps only the ones that happened on the target server (this is the “on” side of from vs on); and means both must be true. Type the quotation marks exactly.

  1. Look at the Documents tab. It should read Documents (5). And look at the histogram — this time it is one tall bar, not a smear.
  2. Make sure the columns user.name, source.ip and logon.type are added, then sort oldest first: click Sort fields 1 and choose Old-New.
Five sessions, one machine — this is the scope of the incident

Write this table into your report now. It is the heart of the case.

Time (UTC)AccountSource (source.ip)Logon typeNote
14:05:00.000jdoe10.0.4.103 (network)the first replay
14:09:00.000asmith10.0.4.103 (network)+4 min
14:13:00.000mchen10.0.4.103 (network)+4 min
14:17:00.000kpatel10.0.4.103 (network)+4 min
14:19:00.000svc_backup10.0.4.103 (network)the service account — same second and same source port as the 4648

Three things to notice, and all three matter:

  • Five different accounts, exactly four minutes apart. That is a machine working through a list of hashes, not a person signing in to places they know. Real administrators reuse the same three servers for months.
  • Every one is logon.type: 3, a network logon, and every one is from the same source address. Nobody was sitting at those machines.
  • The service account is in the list. On its own that is a signal; together with the 4648 on the same source port (49712) and the same second, it is the moment the hash replay produced a session for a non-human identity.

Real Windows behaviour explains why that last row looks like a sixth event: Windows writes the 4648 and the 4624 it produced as two separate records of the same session, the same second, the same source port. So five successful logons and five distinct users agree — and that is why event.code matters so much on the next card.

What a benign answer would have looked like

Suspicious is “five different accounts, one source address, one server, four minutes apart”. Benign is “each account signing in once from its own usual workstation, spread across the working day”. In a false positive you would find the same accounts appearing repeatedly, from their own machines, all day. You found none of that.

Prove it13

Query 4 — the one-shot query, and the trap inside it

4 of 5 queries4 min
Why you are running this query

Query 3 gives you five rows from somewhere on that server. It does not prove they all came from the compromised machine. This query pins that down — and it is the exact filter the detection rule runs.

Do this

Make sure you are still on the auth-* data view, then paste this and press Enter:

Search 4 — type this, then press Enterevent.code: 4624 and host.name: "sec-win-03" and source.ip: "10.0.4.10"

This is Query 3 with one extra clause, source.ip: "10.0.4.10", pinning the results to the single compromised workstation. It is a strictly tighter version: it can only remove rows, never add them.

  1. Add source.port as a column as well. It is the clue that ties the last row to the 4648.
The same five — and now they are attributable
  • Documents (5), identical to Query 3. Because all of that server’s successful logons for the day came from 10.0.4.10. Not most of them. All of them.
  • And 5 is also the alert count. The rule ran the identical filter. You have now found the monitoring system’s answer by hand, and the two agree.
A trap, and it is built into this query on purpose

Drop the event.code clause and search on the two remaining ones alone:

Try this — the wrong answer, on purposehost.name: "sec-win-03" and source.ip: "10.0.4.10"

You get 6, not 5. Try it if you like — then undo it.

The extra row is the 4648 from two cards ago, which happened on the same server from the same address. The event code is the only thing that separates “credentials were handed over” from “a session was created”. If you lose it you will report six logons, be wrong, and not know why.

The setup file checks this number too, and prints it as the trap count, with the event code dropped = 6 so that you know 6 is the trap and 5 is the answer.

The impact14

Query 5 — switch piles, and find the file read

5 of 5 querieschange data view
Why you are running this query

You have proven capability: the attacker got into five accounts on one server. That is serious, but on its own it is still “nothing was actually taken”.

This query looks for intent and impact. And it has to be run against the other data view, because connections are not authentication events — they are in network-*.

Do this

  1. Click the Data view dropdown on the far left and choose network-*.
  2. Your user.name and logon.type columns will disappear on their own — those fields do not exist here. That is normal, not an error.
  3. Replace the contents of the search bar with this and press Enter:
Search 5 — type this, then press Enternetwork.protocol: "smb" and source.ip: "10.0.4.10"

network.protocol: "smb" keeps only SMB, which is Windows file sharing and always uses port 445. source.ip: "10.0.4.10" keeps only connections originating from that same workstation.

  1. Add three more columns from the sidebar, the same way as before: destination.ip, destination.port and network.bytes.
One connection, and it is the whole impact
  • Exactly one SMB session from 10.0.4.10 all day. Not several. One.
  • To 10.0.4.12 on port 445. That is the file server. Note it is not sec-win-03 — the attacker read a different machine, and did it over the network rather than through a logon record.
  • 1,048,576 bytes, which Kibana prints as 1,048,576. That is exactly 1 MB — a suspiciously round number, and 17× larger than any other SMB session in the day’s traffic. Write the byte count down.
  • At 14:25:00.000, six minutes after the last replayed logon and one minute after the service account’s session.

This is what turns a serious alert into a reportable breach. Logons prove capability; an actual one-megabyte data transfer proves intent, and gives you the scope you need for the notification and legal side of the response.

Close it15

Read the file record, and close the loop

the smoking gun

One more click and the case is complete. Open the SMB record and read its message field.

Do this

  1. Click the ⇉ two-diagonal-arrows button on the left of the single row. Not the row — the button.
  2. Scroll the Document panel down to the message field and read it in full.
The message field, in full
The whole sentence, exactly as the log records itSMB read from 10.0.4.10 (ws-fin-01) to 10.0.4.12:445 (srv-file-01), authenticated as CORP\svc_backup. 1048576 bytes transferred in one session.

Four facts in one sentence, and every one of them is new:

  • The file server has a name: srv-file-01. Until now you only had its address, 10.0.4.12.
  • It was authenticated as CORP\svc_backup — the same service account from the 4648, not one of the four human accounts. The attacker did not only use stolen credentials; it used the account that belongs to the backup software, which is the one most likely to have read access to everything.
  • 1,048,576 bytes read in one session. The read completed in a single connection, which is what you expect when a tool is pulling a known set of files rather than a person browsing.
  • It came from ws-fin-01 — the attacker’s own workstation, six minutes after the last replayed logon.
Now close the loop — this is the part that makes the report good

Go back to your Query 3 results. The last row of that burst, the one you found at 14:19, was:

The account that opened the file session too14:19:00.000 svc_backup 10.0.4.10 logon.type 3 port 49712

That is the same account as the file read. The 4648, the session it produced and the one-megabyte SMB read are the same identity, the same second for the first two and six minutes apart for the third.

So the complete chain reads: at 14:05 the workstation replayed a hash as jdoe → at 14:09 as asmith → at 14:13 as mchen → at 14:17 as kpatel → at 14:19 it explicitly supplied the credentials of the backup service account and got a session → at 14:25 it used that service account to read a megabyte off the file server.

It escalated from human accounts to a machine account and then took the data. That is not opportunistic — that is a plan, and it is the most persuasive sentence you can put in your report. And notice that the lab never told you to look for it. You found it by reading a field nobody pointed at.

One more thing worth saying in the report

The estate logs 45 failed logons and 27 account lockouts that day, and not one of them involves 10.0.4.10. Every trace of this attack is in the successful records. A pass-the-hash leaves no failed logon trail at all, because the hash is accepted first time, every time — which is exactly why it is so hard to catch and why this alert exists.

Put it together16

Build the timeline

most important 5 min

This is the most important 5 minutes in the lab. Investigators do not just collect facts — they arrange them so the facts argue the conclusion for them.

Do this

Open a text file (Notepad is fine) and write seven lines, oldest first, copying the times off your own screen. The yellow blank is your work — read it off your table and type it in. The gaps on the right are pre-filled, because gaps are the same in every timezone and they are the actual evidence.

  1. fill in from your screen  →  fill in from your screen
    The burst begins. Successful logon (4624, logon.type 3) for jdoe on sec-win-03 from 10.0.4.10, authentication package NTLM.
  2. fill in  (+4 min)
    Second account. The same pattern for asmith, from the same source, on the same server. Four minutes later to the second.
  3. fill in  (+4 min)
    Third account. mchen, same shape.
  4. fill in  (+4 min)
    Fourth account. kpatel, same shape.
  5. fill in  (+2 min)
    The escalation. Explicit-credential logon (4648, logon.type 3) for the service account svc_backup, subject CORP\ws-fin-01$, package NTLM, source port 49712 — followed in the same second by its companion 4624.
  6. fill in  (+6 min)
    The impact. SMB read from 10.0.4.10 to 10.0.4.12:445 — which is srv-file-01, the file server — 1,048,576 bytes, authenticated as CORP\svc_backup.

The clock times above are UTC, which is how the lab stores them and how this guide’s pictures were taken. If your screen is showing a different offset, write down your numbers instead — what matters is that the six lines stay in this order and keep these gaps: 4, 4, 4, 2 minutes of logons, then 6 minutes to the file read.

The shape of the answer

A quiet baseline of 53 logons spread over 24 hours, and then everything else in the lab happens inside 20 minutes, at 14:05–14:25, in strict order: logon, logon, logon, logon, explicit-credential logon, session, file read. Nothing is hours apart, nothing is days apart.

That tightness is itself evidence. It rules out coincidence, and it rules out routine administration.

Then ask the questions that turn facts into a verdict

QuestionYour answer, and the query that proved it
Who started it?source.ip: 10.0.4.10 (ws-fin-01)
What did they take?1,048,576 bytes from srv-file-01 (10.0.4.12)
How did they get in?pass-the-hash — 5 accounts replayed in 14 minutes, one via 4648
As whom did they end up?the service account svc_backup — a non-human identity
How far did they get?two machines: sec-win-03 and the file server srv-file-01
Why is it not routine?five distinct accounts, one source, one burst, every one logon type 3
The one-sentence verdict

On 22 September 2026 a single workstation, ws-fin-01 (10.0.4.10), replayed stolen NTLM hashes against sec-win-03 and authenticated as five different accounts inside 14 minutes, one of them the service account svc_backup by an explicit-credential logon (event 4648), and six minutes later used that service account to read 1,048,576 bytes from the file server srv-file-01 (10.0.4.12).

That is a true positive. Every clause of that sentence is traceable to one of the five queries you just ran. That is what a finished investigation looks like.

Deliverable17

Write the report, then export it

25 mindo not skip

Nobody reads your screen. This card is the deliverable — it is the thing you hand in, and it is the only place in the guide you type. It has two parts and both go into your submission: Part one is your written report, Part two is the set of figures you checked off your own screen as you went. Neither part has an answer printed next to it. Fill both in, then press EXPORT MY SUBMISSION at the bottom: a finished PDF report lands in your Downloads folder with your name and batch number on the front of it.

Do this yourself, and do it now

If you cannot fill a line in without going back to Kibana, you have not finished the investigation — which is exactly the point. These fields are deliberately empty and stay that way until you type. Nothing here is marked against a model answer; it is marked on whether you found these things.

Both of these are printed at the top of the exported PDF and go into the file name, so the submission is identifiable without you having to say who you are in the report itself. Leave either one blank and the file still exports — it just says [not answered] where your name should be, which is a good reason not to leave them blank.

Part one — your report

1. Summary

What happened

two or three sentences a manager could follow, and no jargon in the first sentence

2. Timeline

When

one line per stage, oldest first, with the times read off your own screen — not off this guide

3. Evidence

How you know

each query you ran, the number it returned, and what that number proved. The number matters as much as the reasoning

4. Impact

What is affected

the accounts, the machines involved, and the volume of data read

5. Verdict

True positive or false positive

state it plainly in the first line, then the whole chain in one paragraph

6. Recommendations

What should happen next

concrete actions in the order you would carry them out. If a change has to be made twice to actually work, say so — that is the single most-missed step in this whole response

Every line below is a number you should be able to point at on your own screen. These travel with your report, so a figure that contradicts your writing gives you away — if Part one and Part two disagree, one of them is wrong, and you want to know which before you hand it in.

Finish18

Tear the lab down

one file1 min

One file removes everything the lab created. Nothing is left running, and nothing of yours is deleted.

Do this

  1. Make sure you have submitted your report. The teardown deletes the data.
  2. Close your browser and every Kibana tab.
  3. In the lab folder, run the teardown file for your system: on Windows, double-click teardown.cmd; on macOS or Linux, run ./teardown.sh in a terminal in that folder (or bash teardown.sh).
  4. It prints the exact list of what it is about to remove, and asks you to confirm (Y or N on Windows, y or n on macOS and Linux). Read the list, then say yes.
  5. It finishes by verifying the removal and telling you what was kept.
The list the teardown file prints before it deletes anything The following will be REMOVED. Nothing else will be touched. container pass-the-hash-001-elasticsearch container pass-the-hash-001-kibana volume pass-the-hash-001_esdata (this holds ALL the lab data) network pass-the-hash-001_lab file .../pass-the-hash-001/docker-compose.yml folder .../elklab-pass-the-hash-001/

Yours will show a different path — a Windows path on Windows, a /var/folders/... or /tmp/ one on a Mac. The five names are the same everywhere, and only the names are ever deleted.

What it will never touch

Every name in that list is derived from the folder name, and nothing else is considered for deletion. In particular:

  • No Docker images are removed. They are large and slow to download, so they are kept and the next setup is fast and works offline.
  • No other container or volume on this machine is touched, so a second lab running beside this one is safe.
  • Your files stay. The log data, the templates, the rule and this guide are all still in the folder afterwards.

The teardown file never runs docker system prune and never removes an image. It says so on screen before it starts, and it means it.

If you would rather just stop it and keep the data

Sometimes you want the lab back tomorrow without waiting for it to reload. Stop the containers but keep everything, and start them again later with one command:

Run this in a terminal, in the lab folderdocker compose -f docker-compose.yml down

Your data lives in the Docker volume, so it survives. Bring it all back with docker compose -f docker-compose.yml up -d, or simply run the setup file again — it is safe to run twice and will not re-import anything.

Running teardown twice is harmless

It checks what is actually there first, tells you there is nothing to do, and exits. It will not complain and it will not delete anything else looking for something to clean up. That matters, because people run it twice to be sure.

Reference19

If something goes wrong

not a steplook me up

Three things account for almost every problem in this lab. Work down the list rather than guessing.

1. The screen is empty and there are no documents

Almost never a broken query. Check, in this order:

  1. Is the data view right? It must say auth-* for queries 1–4 and network-* for query 5.
  2. Is the time range right? If it says Last 15 minutes, the data is older than that and you will see nothing. Click Search entire time range again. This is by far the most common cause, and it happens after pressing F5 or navigating away and back.
  3. Is the query in the bar at all? It should be in plain text, not in a leftover filter row underneath.
If the Alerts page is the empty one

Same cause, different page. An alert is stamped with the time the rule ran, not the time the event happened, so the alerts page starts on Today and the log data is from September 2026. If the Alerts page is empty, set its time picker to Last 24 hours or 1 day and the five come back. The alert card explains the two timestamps, because this one catches everyone out at least once.

2. The counts do not match this guide

You seeWhat it almost certainly means
Double every numberThe data was imported twice. Run the setup file with reset and then it again, which rebuilds the data exactly once.
Nothing for query 5You are still on the auth-* data view. Query 5 has to run on network-*.
6 instead of 5You dropped event.code: 4624, so the 4648 got counted as a logon too. That is the trap on the Query 4 card — and 6 is its correct answer.
Times are hours offThat is your timezone, not a fault. Read the gaps, not the absolute clock times — see the time-range card.
Dates in the past, on a computer years aheadExpected, and not a fault. The log data is a real day in September 2026 and never moves. The rule that raises the alerts only looks back a year, so it keeps finding it.
The sidebar says 0 available fieldsStill a time-range problem. Click Search entire time range.

3. The lab will not start

What the setup file saysWhat to do
docker was not foundDocker is not installed. Ask your instructor, or install Docker Desktop / Docker Engine.
Docker is installed but the engine is not respondingStart Docker and wait until it says Engine running, then run the file again.
curl was not foundEverything in the lab is built with curl. Install it, or move to a machine that has it.
something else is already using port 9200Another lab is running. The script refuses to touch it, correctly. Stop the other one, or run teardown from the folder that owns it.
a container called pass-the-hash-001-elasticsearch already existsThe folder was copied or moved, so a previous copy owns the container. The script shows you the details and stops without deleting anything. Follow the two docker commands it prints, or run the teardown file from the original folder first.
Elasticsearch did not become ready in timeIt prints the last 40 lines of the container log. Usually not enough memory for Docker; close other applications, or give Docker Desktop more memory in its settings.
the auth index holds N documents but this lab ships 274A partial load. The script refuses to import on top of it, because that would create duplicates. Run the setup file with reset.
the rule is installed but has not produced 5 alertsCheck docker logs pass-the-hash-001-kibana for the rule’s execution status. Remember the rule only matches data from the last 365 days.

Two controls that catch people out

  • Clicking a table row does nothing. You need the small ⇉ two-diagonal-arrows button immediately to the left of the @timestamp column. In the Document panel, Escape closes it.
  • The Field statistics tab shows one row per FIELD, not one row per value. It will not give you “three and four” style counts — for an exact number, run the query and read the Documents tab.
The 30-second checklist

Data view right? → Time range says a date, not “Last 15 minutes”? → Query text in the bar? → Number in the Documents tab matches the number this guide quotes? If all four are true and something still looks wrong, press F5 and re-click Search entire time range, then re-run the queries from the top. If Query 1 does not return a large number of documents, your time range is still wrong; if it does, the problem is in the query text rather than in the dates.

Stuck on a step?

Almost every problem in this lab has one of three causes, and all three are on the If it breaks card near the end: the time range reset, the wrong data view, or Docker not running. Go there rather than guessing.
